entries.narration: This chapter turns an informal question into a precise target and a plan for collecting data, and shows how to summarise data without claiming more than they support. Start with the workshop. Someone asks: how good are our chairs? That is not yet a statistical question. Make it precise. The population is every chair made this quarter, six thousand of them. The unit is one chair. The estimand is the fraction that fail the end of line inspection. In this synthetic workshop we happen to know the answer: four hundred and twenty failed, so the parameter p is zero point zero seven. In practice it is unknown, which is why we sample. Take a random sample of a hundred and twenty chairs and count the failures: that fraction is a statistic, p hat. On the left are twenty such samples. Their p hats range from about three percent to almost twelve percent, scattered around the fixed parameter. That is the core distinction of the subject: a parameter is one fixed number describing the population; a statistic is computed from data and changes from sample to sample. Next, what exactly gets recorded.

Before summarising anything, ask what each number is. A dataset records variables on units, and every variable has a measurement scale. Nominal variables are unordered categories, like the type of defect. Ordinal variables are ordered, like a finish grade from one to four, but the gaps between grades are not known to be equal. Interval variables have meaningful differences but an arbitrary zero, like temperature in Celsius. Ratio variables have a true zero, like seat height in millimetres or processing time in minutes, so twice as long really means twice as long. Each variable also has a provenance: an inspector's judgement, a gauge, a wall sensor, a machine log. Now the unit question. On the left, five chairs each had their seat height read four times. The four readings of one chair agree to about half a millimetre, while different chairs differ by about four millimetres. Twenty numbers, but only five units. Treating the readings as twenty independent chairs would overstate how much you know about chairs in general. Next, choosing which units to measure.

How should you choose which units to measure? First you need a sampling frame: the list you actually draw from. Here it is the hundred and twenty batches made over ten days, shown on the left by day. Notice that days differ a lot: some days average under four percent defective, one over ten percent. Now compare three designs that each pick twenty batches. A simple random sample makes every set of twenty equally likely. A stratified sample takes two batches at random from every day. A cluster sample picks two whole days at random and takes ten batches from each, which is often cheaper. All three are unbiased: averaged over many repetitions they hit the population mean of six point six six percent. But their precision differs. Over ten thousand simulated repetitions, the stratified estimate has a standard error of about zero point two, simple random about zero point four five, and the cluster estimate about one point three, because two days can easily both be unusual, like days five and seven here. One limit no design fixes: units missing from the frame cannot be sampled at all. Next, other ways data can mislead.

Can a large, carefully computed average still be wrong? Yes, if the data are systematically unlike the population. That is bias, and unlike random error it does not shrink with more data. It has several common sources. Selection: units enter the data in a way linked to the outcome, such as timing only the batches operators flag as troublesome. Nonresponse: some selected units never report, such as a night shift that skips the survey. Measurement: an instrument or rule reads off target, such as a gauge knocked out of calibration. And missingness: values that are absent for reasons connected to the values themselves. On the left is that last case. Of four hundred jobs, those that take longer than twenty minutes run past the end of the shift, and only forty percent of them get logged. The grey bars are all jobs; the teal bars are those in the log. The long tail is thinned out, so the logged average is eleven point seven four minutes when the truth is twelve point six four. Logging more jobs the same way would only reproduce the gap more precisely. Next, two kinds of randomness.

Chance enters a study in two different ways, and they answer different questions. Random sampling decides which units from a population get studied. It lets you generalise from the sample to that population. Random assignment decides which treatment each studied unit receives. It lets you attribute differences in outcome to the treatment, because nothing else systematically differs between the groups. The four combinations on the left follow. With both, you can make causal claims about the whole population. With assignment only, causal claims hold for the units in the study. With sampling only, you can describe the population but not explain it. With neither, you have an association among the units you happened to see. The table applies this to the workshop. Running setting A early in the week and B later confounds the setting with the day. Drawing the setting by lot for each batch supports a causal comparison for those batches. And measuring one chair ten times under setting B is still one chair: the experimental unit is whatever was assigned, not however many readings it yields. Next, describing what was measured.

How should forty processing times be summarised? Start by looking. The histogram on the left shows most jobs taking between seven and sixteen minutes, a long tail to the right, and one job at sixty three minutes, when a feed jammed. The shape is single peaked and right skewed. Shape matters because summaries respond to it differently. The mean, fourteen point oh seven minutes, is pulled toward the tail; the median, ten point seven five, sits in the middle of the typical jobs. The table shows what happens when the jammed job is removed. The mean drops by more than a minute and the standard deviation falls from about ten to under seven, while the median and the interquartile range barely change. Summaries that barely react to a few extreme values are called resistant. But resistant does not mean correct. If the question is how much machine time the jobs consumed in total, the mean is exactly the right estimand, and the jam is part of the answer. So choose summaries from the question, then report how sensitive they are to the extreme values. Next, relationships between variables, and a trap.

Is setting B better or worse than setting A? Look at one month of inspections. For chairs, B's defect rate is eight percent against A's ten. For tables, B's is twenty five percent against A's thirty. B is better for both products. Yet overall, A's rate is fifteen percent and B's is almost twenty one. How can B be better within every group and worse in total? Because an overall rate is a weighted average of the product rates, and the weights are each setting's product mix. Setting A ran mostly chairs, the easy product; setting B ran mostly tables, the hard one. On the left, each setting's overall rate is drawn as a function of the share of chairs. B's line is below A's everywhere, but the two settings sit at very different points along it. This reversal is called Simpson's paradox. Which comparison is right depends on the question, and the product is a lurking variable that must be considered. More generally, patterns found by slicing data many ways are leads to investigate, not conclusions. Next, the limits of what any of this supports.

How far can a well run study be trusted? Only as far as the population and period it actually sampled. Suppose a careful random sample of weeks one to four put the defect rate at about six and a half percent. That claim is well supported for those weeks. In week seven the timber supplier changed, and the rate rose to about ten and a half percent. On the left, the shaded window is what the study saw; the later weeks are a different population. Claims about now, or about the night shift that was never sampled, go beyond the evidence. Collection has ethical limits too. Gather only what the question needs, keep people's identities out of shared files unless there is consent and a reason, and report how the data were gathered as well as what they showed, so others can judge the limits for themselves. That completes the chapter. You can state a statistical question with its unit and population, explain how the way data were collected limits what they show, and choose summaries that do not claim too much. Next, probability provides a model for the uncertainty observed in data.

This chapter builds probability models and calculates with them under explicit assumptions, including how to update probabilities when new information arrives. Start with the building blocks. The sample space is the list of everything that could happen. Inspect three chairs, and each is good or defective, so there are two times two times two, eight outcomes. An event is any set of those outcomes, such as at least one chair is defective. A probability assigns each event a number, and it must follow three rules: no probability is negative, the whole sample space has probability one, and probabilities of events that cannot happen together add. Everything else follows from these, including that the probability of not A is one minus the probability of A. Now a model. Suppose each chair is defective with probability seven percent, independently of the others. Then all three are good with probability zero point nine three cubed, about zero point eight. So at least one is defective with probability about zero point two. On the left, the outcomes grouped by the number of defectives. Notice they are far from equally likely. Next, combining events.

How do you count chairs that can fail in more than one way? Treat events as sets. A union B means A or B or both; A intersect B means both; the complement means not A. This quarter, a hundred and fifty chairs failed on the seat, a hundred and eighty on joints and a hundred and eighty on finish. Adding those gives five hundred and ten, but that is too many, because a chair with a bad seat and a bad joint was counted twice. Inclusion exclusion fixes the count. For two events, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap once. For three, add the three singles, subtract the three pairwise overlaps, and add back the triple overlap, which the subtraction removed once too often. Five hundred and ten, minus a hundred and five, plus fifteen, gives four hundred and twenty defective chairs, a probability of seven percent. On the left, each region of the diagram holds its own count. Those seven regions, together with the chairs with no defect, form a partition: every chair falls in exactly one piece, so the pieces add up to all six thousand. Next, counting outcomes systematically.

When every outcome is equally likely, a probability is just a count divided by a count. The work is in counting correctly. Three rules cover most cases. Choosing k items in order with replacement gives n to the k possibilities. In order without replacement, n times n minus one, and so on, k times. And unordered without replacement, the number of subsets, n choose k. Take a batch of twenty chairs with three defective, and draw five at random without replacement. There are fifteen thousand five hundred and four possible subsets of five. Those that avoid all three defective chairs are subsets of the seventeen good ones: six thousand one hundred and eighty eight. So the chance the sample contains no defective chair is about zero point four. On the left, that probability for every sample size, compared with drawing with replacement. The curves differ because, without replacement, each good chair removed makes the remaining batch slightly richer in defects. And remember the assumption behind the division: every subset equally likely. Taking the five chairs on top of the pallet is not that. Next, probabilities that change as information arrives.

How should a probability change when you learn something? Conditional probability answers it. The probability of B given A is the probability of both, divided by the probability of A: you restrict attention to the outcomes where A happened and renormalise. Rearranged, it becomes the multiplication rule: the probability of A and B is the probability of A times the probability of B given A. A tree applies this one branch at a time. Draw two chairs from the batch of twenty with three defective. The first is defective with probability three twentieths. If it was, two defective chairs remain among nineteen, so the second is defective with probability two nineteenths; if the first was good, three nineteenths. Multiply along each path: both defective has probability about zero point zero one six. Add across paths that end the same way: the second chair is defective with probability zero point zero one six plus zero point one three four, which is exactly three twentieths. Unconditionally, the second draw is no different from the first. Only once you know the first result does it change. Next, reversing a condition.

If the end of line check flags a chair, how likely is it really defective? This needs two tools. Total probability splits an event across a partition: a flag comes either from a defective chair or from a good one, so add the two routes. Bayes' rule then reverses the condition: the probability of defective given flagged equals the probability of flagged given defective, times the probability of defective, divided by the probability of a flag. The numbers are easiest as expected counts. Picture ten thousand chairs. Seven percent, seven hundred, are defective, and the check flags ninety percent of them: six hundred and thirty. Of the nine thousand three hundred good chairs, it flags five percent: four hundred and sixty five. So one thousand and ninety five chairs are flagged, and six hundred and thirty of those are truly defective. The probability that a flagged chair is defective is about fifty eight percent, far below the ninety percent sensitivity. The many good chairs produce almost as many flags as the few defective ones. And a chair that passes is defective with probability under one percent. Next, when knowing one event says nothing about another.

When does knowing one event tell you nothing about another? When they are independent: the probability of both equals the product of their probabilities, or equivalently, conditioning on one leaves the other unchanged. On the left are two workshops with the same overall defect rate of seven percent. In the first, day and night shifts both run at seven percent, so a chair's shift tells you nothing about whether it is defective: independent. In the second, the day shift runs at five percent and the night shift at ten. The overall rate is the same, but now shift and defects are dependent. Do not confuse independence with exclusivity. Exclusive events cannot happen together, like no defect and a seat defect. Learning one rules out the other, which is about as dependent as events can be. A subtler idea is conditional independence. Two inspectors might make errors independently once the chair's true state is fixed. Yet overall, their flags are strongly dependent: both flag about six percent of chairs, five times the product of their separate rates, because both are reacting to the same defective chairs. Next, a common reversal error.

What does a flag mean if defects become rarer? The check catches ninety percent of defective chairs, and that number describes the check. It is the probability of a flag given a defect. What an inspector wants is the reverse: the probability of a defect given a flag. At the workshop's seven percent defect rate, that is fifty eight percent, not ninety. Treating one conditional probability as the other is the reversal error, and it is one of the most common mistakes in reasoning about evidence. The curves on the left show why the base rate matters. As defects become rarer, the good chairs vastly outnumber the defective ones, and even a small false positive rate produces more false flags than true ones. At a one percent defect rate, a flagged chair is defective only about fifteen percent of the time; at a tenth of a percent, under two percent. Lowering the false positive rate to one percent, the teal curve, helps a lot: fifty eight percent becomes eighty seven. The lesson is general: accuracy figures describe a test, but what a positive result means depends on how common the condition is. Next, events with probability zero.

Can something with probability zero happen? For continuous quantities, it happens every time. Model a job's processing time as a continuous quantity with a median of twelve minutes. The probability it lands between eleven and thirteen minutes is about thirteen percent. Between eleven point nine and twelve point one, about one point three percent. Keep shrinking the interval and the probability shrinks with it, toward zero. So the probability that the time is exactly twelve minutes, to infinitely many decimal places, is zero. Yet some exact value always occurs. Probability zero is not the same as impossible. What stays meaningful is the ratio of probability to interval width, which settles at about zero point zero six six five per minute. That is the density at twelve: a rate, not a probability. Probabilities come from areas under the density curve. This also marks a boundary for conditioning. The definition P of A given B divides by P of B, which fails when B has probability zero, so conditioning on an exact time needs densities, which come later. That completes the chapter. Next, random variables express uncertain quantities under these probability rules.

This chapter describes uncertain quantities with probability models, and connects those models to averages, variability, tails and the reference distributions used later for inference. A random variable is a rule that attaches a number to each outcome. Count the defective chairs in a random sample of ten, and you have a random variable X. Its support is the set of values it can take, zero to ten, and its distribution says how probability is spread over them. For a discrete variable like this one, the mass function gives the probability of each value. Under a binomial model with a seven percent defect rate, there is a forty eight percent chance of no defectives and a thirty six percent chance of exactly one. The stems on the left show the mass function. The orange steps show the cumulative distribution function, the probability of being at most x. It works for every kind of variable. For discrete variables it rises in steps, one for each value, by that value's mass. For continuous variables it rises smoothly, and its slope is the density. Either way, the probability of an interval is a difference of two CDF values. Next, summarising a distribution with one or two numbers.

What single number best summarises a random quantity? Usually its expectation: the sum of each value times its probability. It is the long run average over many repetitions, and the balance point of the distribution. For defective chairs in a batch of twenty, with a seven percent rate, the expectation is twenty times zero point zero seven, one point four. No batch ever has one point four defective chairs; an expectation need not be a possible value. The variance measures spread around it: the expected squared distance from the mean, here one point three, so the standard deviation is about one point one four. For linear rules, expectation passes straight through: adding a constant shifts the mean, and multiplying by b multiplies the mean by b and the variance by b squared. But many real quantities are nonlinear. Suppose rework costs ten pounds to set up whenever a batch has any defect, plus fifteen per defective chair. The expected cost is ten times the probability of any defect, plus fifteen times one point four: twenty eight pounds sixty six. Plugging the average count into the rule instead gives thirty one pounds, which is wrong. Next, the binomial family.

Which model fits a count of defectives in a sample? Start with a Bernoulli trial: one inspection, defective or not, with probability p. The binomial distribution counts the defectives in n such trials, and it rests on three assumptions: a fixed number of trials, the same probability every time, and independence between trials. Drawing chairs from a large production run comes close. Drawing from a small batch does not. Take five chairs from the batch of twenty that contains three defective. Without replacement, each draw changes the batch, so the draws are dependent, and the exact model is the hypergeometric: count subsets, as in chapter two. On the left, the two models side by side. They agree on the mean, five times three twentieths, zero point seven five. But the hypergeometric is less spread out, with variance zero point five against zero point six four, because sampling without replacement cannot keep hitting the same defective chairs. The ratio is the finite population correction, fifteen nineteenths. When the sample is a small fraction of the population, like five chairs from six thousand, the correction is nearly one, and the binomial is an excellent approximation. Next, waiting times and rare counts.

How long until the first defective chair? Inspect chairs one by one, each defective with probability seven percent, independently. The number of inspections up to and including the first defective follows a geometric distribution. Its most likely value is one: the very first chair. Yet its median is ten and its mean is one over p, about fourteen. And eleven percent of the time you inspect more than thirty chairs before seeing a defect. The long right tail on the left is why a run of good chairs is weak evidence that the defect rate has fallen. A caution about conventions: some textbooks and software count the good chairs before the first defective instead, which shifts everything down by one, to a mean of thirteen point three. State which you mean. The Poisson distribution counts events in a fixed amount of space or time, when they occur independently at a steady rate, such as surface flaws on a panel. With a mean of one and a half flaws per panel, the chance of a flawless panel is about twenty two percent. A Poisson's variance equals its mean, which is worth checking against data, because clustered flaws break it. Next, continuous models.

How do you calculate with a continuous model? Probabilities are areas under the density curve. The normal distribution is the most used. Model seat height as normal with mean four hundred and fifty millimetres and standard deviation three point nine, the spread between chairs from chapter one. The specification allows four hundred and forty four to four hundred and fifty six. To find the share within it, standardise: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation. The limits become minus and plus one point five four standard units, and the standard normal table, or software, gives an area of about zero point eight eight, the shaded region on the left. About six percent of seats are too high. The exponential distribution models waiting times between events that occur at a steady rate, like machine stoppages, averaging forty minutes apart. The chance of going an hour without one is about twenty two percent. It is memoryless: having already run thirty minutes without a stoppage, the chance of reaching sixty is the same as the chance of lasting thirty more from scratch. One warning: density values are not probabilities, and can exceed one. Only areas are probabilities. Next, choosing a family.

Which model should describe processing times? Start with what values are possible. Times are positive, so a model that allows negative times is wrong in principle. On the left are the forty processing times as a histogram, with two fitted curves. The normal curve, matched to the sample mean and standard deviation, puts almost nine percent of its probability below zero minutes, and it is too thin in the long right tail. The lognormal, a distribution whose logarithm is normal, lives on positive values and is right skewed, like the data. Fitted by maximum likelihood, it has a median of about eleven point eight minutes, and its log likelihood is much higher, which means the data are far more probable under it. Families can be organised by support: lognormal, gamma and exponential for positive quantities, beta for proportions between zero and one, normal and t for symmetric unbounded ones. Then check the model where the decision lies. If the question is how often a job takes over forty minutes, the data say two and a half percent, the lognormal says about two, and the normal says under one: a fourfold understatement. Next, tails, quantiles and moments.

Does every distribution have a mean? No, and this matters more than it sounds. A quantile always exists: the value with a given share of probability below it. A mean exists only if the tail thins out fast enough. Pareto distributions make this concrete: the chance of exceeding x falls like x to the minus alpha. On the left are running means of a hundred thousand simulated draws for three tail indices. With alpha three, the running mean settles at one point five. With alpha one point five, the mean is three but the variance is infinite, and the running mean wanders before settling. With alpha one, there is no mean at all, and the running mean keeps jumping upward whenever a huge draw arrives, however many draws you take. Every sample has a mean; whether it estimates anything depends on the tail. Distributions can also be mixed. Repair cost per chair is zero for the ninety three percent that pass, a point mass, and a continuous cost for the rest. Its median is zero, its ninety fifth percentile about eighteen pounds, and its mean two pounds ten. Which summary to report depends on the question. Next, distributions that inference relies on.

Some distributions are rarely used to model raw data, yet appear constantly in inference. They are reference distributions for statistics computed from normal samples. The t distribution describes a standardised sample mean when the standard deviation is estimated from the same data. The chi square describes sums of squared standard normals, and so sample variances. The F describes a ratio of two independent variance estimates. Each is indexed by degrees of freedom, roughly the amount of independent information behind the estimate. On the left, t densities with two, five and thirty degrees of freedom against the standard normal. With few degrees of freedom the tails are much heavier: the chance of a value beyond plus or minus two is eighteen percent with two degrees of freedom, against under five percent for the normal. The ninety seven point five percent point falls from four point three with two degrees of freedom to two point oh four with thirty, approaching the normal's one point nine six. That completes the chapter. You can choose and calculate with discrete and continuous models, and recognise unsupported tail and moment assumptions. Next, several quantities require a joint model and explicit dependence reasoning.

This chapter models several uncertain quantities at once, and separates association from independence. A joint distribution describes variables together: which combinations of values occur, and how likely each combination is. For two discrete variables, it is a table. Inspect a thousand items, classify each by product and by defect status, and the nine cell proportions form a joint distribution: fifty five and a half percent are chairs with no defect, one and a half percent are tables with a major defect, and all nine add up to one. For continuous variables, the joint distribution is a density over the plane, and probabilities are volumes under it. On the left, two hundred jobs, each with its cutting time and its total processing time. Because the total includes the cutting, every job lies above the line where the two are equal. That region is the support, and it is not a rectangle. Constraints like this are part of the joint model. If you modelled cutting time and total time separately and paired values at random, you would create impossible jobs that finish before they are cut. Next, recovering one variable's distribution from the joint.

How do you get one variable's distribution from a joint model? Sum out the other one. That gives the marginal distribution, named because in a table it appears in the margins. Add along each row of the product by defect table: chairs make up sixty percent of items, tables thirty, stools ten. Add down each column: ninety point six percent have no defect, six point six percent a minor defect, two point eight a major one. On the left are both marginal distributions, each obtained by summing over the other variable. For continuous variables the sum becomes an integral: the marginal density of X at a value x integrates the joint density over all y. The support matters here, because it sets the limits. For cutting time and total time, the integral over y starts at x, since the total can never be less than the cutting time. One important limitation: margins do not determine the joint distribution. Many different tables have exactly these row and column totals, with very different relationships between product and defect. Knowing each variable on its own is not knowing how they go together. Next, how one variable's distribution changes when the other is known.

How does defect status depend on the product? Look at one row of the joint table and rescale it so it sums to one. That is the conditional distribution of defect status given the product. Among chairs, ninety two and a half percent have no defect, five and a half percent a minor one, two percent a major one. Tables are worse: ten percent minor and five percent major. Stools are best. On the left, the minor and major rates for each product side by side. Now attach a cost: nothing for no defect, eight pounds for minor, forty for major. The conditional expectation of cost given the product averages the costs using that product's row: one pound twenty four for a chair, two pounds eighty for a table, sixty four pence for a stool. Notice that this conditional expectation depends on the product, so it is itself a random quantity, a function of which product turns up. And averaging it, with weights sixty, thirty and ten percent, gives back the overall expected cost, one pound sixty five. Using that overall figure for a batch of tables would understate the cost by more than a pound a piece. Next, when the rows are all alike.

What would it mean for product and defect status to be unrelated? Independence means the joint distribution factors into its margins: every cell equals its row probability times its column probability. Equivalently, every conditional row is the same as the marginal, so the defect distribution does not depend on the product. Check it. If they were independent, tables with a major defect would make up thirty percent times two point eight percent, about point eight four percent of items. The table shows one and a half percent, nearly double. Chairs with a minor defect are three point three percent, against about four percent under independence. On the left, each defective cell plotted against its independence prediction. Under independence they would all sit on the diagonal. They do not, so product and defect status are dependent. The definition carries over to densities: the joint density must factor into the product of the marginal densities. One consequence is worth remembering. The support must then be a product set, a rectangle. Cutting time and total time have a triangular support, so they cannot be independent: learning that cutting took eight minutes rules out a total of seven. Next, measuring how strongly variables move together.

How strongly do two quantities move together? Covariance measures it: the expected product of their deviations from their means. When both tend to be above their means together, or below together, the products are positive and so is the covariance. Correlation divides by both standard deviations, giving a unit free number between minus one and one. For the two hundred jobs, cutting time has variance three point eight, total time fourteen point three, and their covariance is about four point eight square minutes. The correlation is about zero point six five: a strong positive linear association, visible in the scatter on the left. The least squares line has slope equal to covariance over the variance of X, about one point two five. Arrange the variances and covariance in a square and you have the covariance matrix: spreads on the diagonal, joint movement off it. In this model the total is cutting time plus an independent finishing time, so in theory the covariance equals the variance of X; the sample's gap is sampling noise. A crucial limit: correlation sees only straight line association. A deviation and its square are completely dependent, yet their correlation is about zero. Next, what dependence does to totals.

How uncertain is a total, or an average, of several quantities? Expectations always add. Variances add only when the quantities are uncorrelated; otherwise each pair contributes twice its covariance. Take the batch defect rates from chapter one. Each is seven percent plus a day effect with variance four, plus batch noise with variance one, so each batch has variance five. Two batches from different days are independent. Two batches from the same day share the day effect, so their covariance is four. Now average n batches. Spread over different days, the variance of the average is five over n, and it shrinks toward zero as n grows: the teal curve on the left. All from the same day, the shared day effect never averages out. The variance approaches four, so the standard deviation of the average levels off near two percentage points, the pink curve. Twelve batches from one day give a standard deviation of about two, against about zero point six five for twelve batches from twelve days. This is exactly why the cluster sample in chapter one was so imprecise, and why treating same day batches as independent observations understates the uncertainty threefold. Next, splitting variance into parts.

Where does variability come from? The law of total variance answers that by splitting it into parts. First, total expectation: the overall mean is the average of the group means. Grouping the hundred and twenty batches by day, each day has its own mean, the orange points on the left, and averaging those day means gives the overall six point six six percent. Now variance. The total variance equals the average variance within groups, plus the variance between the group means. Computed from the batches, the average within day variance is about zero point nine four, and the variance of the day means is about three point seven eight. Together they make the total, four point seven two, exactly. So about eighty percent of the variation in batch defect rates is between days, and only twenty percent within a day. The model that generated these data has one and four, so the split is recovered well. The point is practical. The decomposition tells you where variation lives, and so where to act. Tightening control from batch to batch within a day could remove at most a fifth of the variance; the day level causes drive the rest. Next, mixtures and the multivariate normal.

Two structures recur whenever data come from groups or from several correlated measurements. A mixture picks a group at random, then draws a value from that group. Job times are a mixture: sixty percent chairs, averaging about ten and a half minutes, and forty percent tables, averaging about twenty one. The mixture's mean is the weighted average, about fourteen point six. Its variance, about forty nine, is the law of total variance again: the average spread within the groups plus the spread between the group means. A mixture can have two peaks, and then no single typical job exists. The multivariate normal is the standard model for several correlated continuous measurements, and it is determined entirely by the means and the covariance matrix. On the left, standardised bivariate normals. Contours of equal density are ellipses. With correlation zero they are circles, and for the normal, uncorrelated really does mean independent. With correlation zero point eight, the ellipses stretch along the diagonal. The inner contour holds thirty nine percent of the probability, the outer eighty six. That completes the chapter. You can derive marginal and conditional summaries and explain dependence. Next, repeated sampling turns joint models into distributions of statistics.

This chapter explains how probability models determine the behaviour of statistics over repeated samples, and how simulation can investigate a model when formulas run out. The first tool is transformation. If a quantity Y is a function of X, its distribution follows from X's. The most reliable route is the CDF method: write the probability that Y is at most y in terms of X, and work it out. Take a uniform random number U between zero and one, and set X equal to minus forty times the log of U. X exceeds x exactly when U is below e to the minus x over forty, which has probability e to the minus x over forty. That is the exponential distribution with mean forty, the stoppage model from chapter three. This inverse CDF trick is how simulators turn uniform random numbers into draws from other distributions. On the left, two thousand such draws, matching the derived density. For monotone functions there is also a density shortcut, but it needs a Jacobian factor: the derivative that measures how the transformation stretches the axis. Leaving it out is the most common error in transforming densities. Next, the distribution of a statistic across samples.

How much would an estimate change if the study were repeated? That variation is described by the sampling distribution: the distribution of a statistic across all the samples the design could have produced. For the defect proportion from samples of a hundred and twenty chairs, it is known exactly. The count of defectives is binomial, so p hat has stems at every possible proportion, shown on the left. The distribution is centred on the true seven percent, so p hat is unbiased. Its standard deviation, the standard error, is the square root of p times one minus p over n, about two point three percentage points. Below the stems are chapter one's twenty actual samples, scattered much as the distribution predicts; their standard deviation was about one point eight points. The standard error shrinks like one over the square root of n: four times the sample size halves it. Two cautions. The standard error describes variation over hypothetical repeated samples under a stated design. It does not tell you how far your one estimate is from the truth. And it says nothing about bias, such as the missing long jobs of chapter one. Next, guarantees that hold with very few assumptions.

Can anything be said about a tail probability without assuming a model shape? Yes, if a mean or a variance is known, though not much. Markov's inequality says that a non negative quantity exceeds t with probability at most its mean divided by t. Chebyshev's inequality says that a quantity lands k or more away from its mean with probability at most its variance over k squared. Both are guaranteed for every distribution with the needed moment. Apply them to processing times, with mean thirteen point six and standard deviation seven and a quarter minutes. The chance of a job taking forty minutes or more is at most thirty four percent by Markov and seven and a half percent by Chebyshev. The lognormal model says under one percent. On the left, on a log scale, the bounds sit far above the model's answer at every threshold, and at twenty minutes Chebyshev's bound exceeds one, which says nothing at all. So bounds are safe but loose. They are useful when the shape is genuinely unknown and a guarantee is needed, and Chebyshev's is the key step in proving the law of large numbers, which comes next.

What happens to an average as the sample grows? Two different theorems answer two different questions. The law of large numbers says the sample mean settles at the true mean. A running mean of simulated processing times is about seventeen after ten jobs, fourteen after a hundred, and thirteen point seven after a thousand, closing in on the true thirteen point six. The central limit theorem describes how the mean fluctuates on the way there: approximately normally, with standard deviation sigma over the square root of n. On the left, the distribution of the mean of four processing times, in pink, is still clearly skewed. The mean of thirty, in teal, is narrower, with standard deviation about one point three, and close to its normal approximation. Keep the claims separate. The law of large numbers needs only a finite mean. The central limit theorem needs a finite variance, and its approximately depends on both n and how skewed the data are. Two warnings. The theorem concerns the mean, not the data: individual jobs stay skewed however many you collect. And tails converge slowest: with thirty jobs, the chance of a mean more than two standard errors high is still three percent, not two point three. Next, when these results fail.

When do the standard results mislead? The familiar standard error and the normal approximation rest on three conditions: independent observations, a finite variance, and a sample that is a small part of the population. Each can fail. On the left, heavy tails. Draw thirty values from a Pareto distribution with tail index one and a half: its mean is three but its variance is infinite. Ten thousand such sample means form a strongly skewed distribution. Most fall below the true mean, because the rare enormous values that balance them out usually do not appear, and when one does it drags that sample's mean far above. A normal curve with the same centre has the wrong shape entirely. Dependence fails differently, as chapter four showed: twelve batches from one day have a standard error three times the independent formula. The third condition goes the other way. Sampling without replacement from a finite population gives a smaller standard error, by the square root of N minus n over N minus one. For a hundred and twenty chairs out of six thousand that factor is zero point nine nine, ignorable. Sampling half the population, it is zero point seven one. A large n never rescues a broken assumption. Next, simulation.

What if a probability has no formula? Simulate. Monte Carlo estimation generates the model's random outcome many times and averages. Here is a workshop question: if each of a shift's eight jobs takes a lognormal time with median twelve minutes, how likely is the shift to run over two hours? The sum of lognormals has no closed form, so the code on the right simulates ten thousand shifts, adds up each shift's eight times, and records the fraction over a hundred and twenty minutes: about twenty six percent. The law of large numbers says this fraction converges to the true probability. The central limit theorem gives its uncertainty: a Monte Carlo standard error of the square root of p hat times one minus p hat over R, about zero point zero zero four four. So report zero point two six three, plus or minus about zero point zero zero nine. On the left, the running estimate and its uncertainty band narrowing as replications accumulate, around the value from a two million replication run. One limit dominates everything else. Monte Carlo error measures the simulation, not the model. If the times are dependent within a shift, the answer is precisely wrong. Next, planning a simulation's size.

How many replications are enough? Monte Carlo error shrinks like one over the square root of R, so precision is expensive: four times the replications halves the standard error. On the left, the shift simulation was rerun two hundred times with different seeds at each of three budgets. With a thousand replications the estimates spread with a standard deviation of about zero point zero one three; with four thousand, about zero point zero zero six five; with sixteen thousand, zero point zero zero three five. The theoretical curve, square root of p times one minus p over R, matches. This gives a planning rule: to get within plus or minus delta at two standard errors, you need about four p times one minus p over delta squared replications. Pinning this probability to within zero point zero zero two needs nearly two hundred thousand runs. Rare events are harder still, because the error relative to a small probability is large. Finally, seeds. A seed fixes the stream of random numbers, so a run can be reproduced exactly. Record it and report it. Re running with new seeds until the answer looks favourable is a form of selective reporting. Next, checking a simulator before trusting it.

How do you know a simulation is right? Test it where the answer is known. A simulator for batch defect counts should reproduce the binomial distribution exactly, so run it ten thousand times and compare. On the left, the simulated proportions and the exact probabilities agree closely at every count. The probability of three or more defective chairs is zero point one five seven eight simulated and zero point one six one zero exact, a gap of under one Monte Carlo standard error. The same simulator's mean shift length is within one point three standard errors of its exact value. Agreement within Monte Carlo error is the test; a gap of five standard errors would mean a bug or a mistaken formula. Simulation reproduces a model's consequences, and comparing them with analytic results can expose errors in either. But no amount of simulation shows that the model describes the workshop. That needs data, and the methods of the coming chapters. That completes the chapter. You can explain a sampling distribution, distinguish the law of large numbers from the central limit theorem, and report a simulation with its uncertainty. Next, these distributions and simulations prepare inference about unknown parameters.

This chapter constructs estimators, judges their quality, and shows how much they depend on the model. A model describes how the data could have arisen, with unknown parameters. An estimator is a rule for turning data into a guess at a parameter: the sample proportion for a defect rate, the sample mean and standard deviation for seat heights. Before any data arrive, an estimator is a random variable with a sampling distribution; applied to one dataset, it gives a number, the estimate. There is a precondition for estimation at all: identifiability. Different parameter values must produce different distributions of data. Suppose the workshop records only whether the end of line check flagged each chair. The flag rate depends on both the true defect rate and the check's sensitivity. On the left, every combination on the curve predicts exactly the same flag rate, about eleven percent. A seven percent defect rate with ninety percent sensitivity fits as well as fifteen percent with forty five. The data cannot choose. No method or sample size fixes this; the design must, for example by re inspecting a subsample with a reliable method. Next, measuring how good an estimator is.

What makes one estimator better than another? Look at its sampling distribution. Bias is how far its average sits from the true value; variance is how much it scatters around that average. Mean squared error combines the two: bias squared plus variance. Take the variance of seat heights, fifteen point two one, estimated from samples of only five chairs. The usual sample variance divides the sum of squared deviations by n minus one, and it is unbiased. Dividing by n instead gives an estimator whose average is only twelve point one seven: biased low by three. On the left, twenty thousand simulated samples show both sampling distributions. The surprise is in the table. The biased estimator has the smaller mean squared error, eighty three against a hundred and sixteen, because dividing by the larger n shrinks its variance more than the bias costs. So unbiased does not mean closer. Both estimators are consistent: their bias, minus sigma squared over n, vanishes as the sample grows, and both converge to the truth. Unbiasedness is a property at a fixed sample size; consistency is about large samples. Choose by the error that matters for the use. Next, a simple general recipe for estimators.

Is there a simple general way to estimate a model's parameters? The method of moments: write the model's mean and variance in terms of its parameters, set them equal to the sample mean and variance, and solve. Fit a gamma model to the forty processing times. A gamma with shape k and scale theta has mean k theta and variance k theta squared. The sample mean is fourteen point oh seven and the sample variance a hundred and eight. Dividing the variance by the mean gives a scale of seven point six five, and the shape follows: one point eight four. It takes two lines of algebra. On the left, compare it with the maximum likelihood fit, which has a shape of two point nine four. Both match the sample mean, but the moment fit is wider and more skewed, and its log likelihood is lower, so it explains the data less well. The reason is the one sixty three minute jammed job. The sample variance is inflated by it, and the moment fit, which uses only the mean and variance, follows. Moment estimators are quick and usually consistent, but they inherit the fragility of the summaries they use. Next, the principle behind the better fit.

Which values of the defect rate are consistent with finding nine defective chairs in a hundred and twenty? The likelihood function answers it. Take the probability of the observed data under the model, here p to the ninth times one minus p to the hundred and eleventh, and read it as a function of p with the data held fixed. On the left, scaled so its peak is one. It is largest at p equal to nought point oh seven five, the sample proportion. At five percent it is about half as large, meaning the data are half as probable if the true rate were five percent. At three percent it is a twentieth. The values whose likelihood is at least an eighth of the maximum run from about three and a half to thirteen percent, a likelihood interval. Be careful about what the curve is not. It is not a probability distribution for p: its area need not be one, and only ratios between its values have meaning. Saying that nought point oh seven five is the most probable value of p is a common misreading; the accurate statement is that it makes the observed data most probable. Turning a likelihood into probabilities for p needs a prior, the subject of chapter eleven. Next, maximising it.

How do you find the parameter value that best explains the data? Maximise the likelihood, or more conveniently its logarithm, which turns products into sums and has the same maximiser. For inspections, the log likelihood is x times log p plus n minus x times log of one minus p. Set its derivative to zero, and the answer is p hat equals x over n: nine over a hundred and twenty, nought point oh seven five. The sample proportion is the maximum likelihood estimate. The peak's sharpness carries the precision. On the left, the log likelihood relative to its peak. A sharply curved peak means the data rule out nearby values strongly. The curvature at the peak, called the observed information, is n over p hat times one minus p hat, about seventeen hundred, and one over its square root gives the standard error, about nought point oh two four, the same as the familiar formula. The orange curve is the quadratic approximation that this standard error implies. It is close near the peak, but the true log likelihood is skewed: it falls faster towards zero than towards higher rates. That asymmetry is lost by symmetric intervals built from curvature alone, a point that returns in chapter seven. Next, examples and a boundary case.

The maximum likelihood recipe reproduces most familiar estimators. For a normal mean it gives the sample mean; for a normal variance, the version that divides by n, which we saw is biased. For a Poisson rate it gives the total count divided by the total exposure: twenty seven flaws on eighteen panels is one and a half flaws per panel. Rates always need their exposure; a count of defects per day means nothing without knowing how many hours ran. Now a case where the recipe needs care. Inspect forty chairs and find no defects. The likelihood is one minus p to the fortieth, shown on the left, and it is largest at p equals zero, on the boundary of the parameter space. The derivative is not zero there, and the usual curvature formula gives a standard error of zero, implying certainty that the rate is exactly zero. That is absurd: forty good chairs are entirely consistent with a few percent defective. Report an upper bound instead. The exact ninety five percent upper bound is about seven percent, and the quick rule of three, three over n, gives seven and a half. Large sample formulas assume the estimate is safely inside the parameter space. Next, how much information a summary keeps.

How much does a summary throw away? A statistic is sufficient if, under the model, it carries all the information the sample has about the parameter. For inspections, the count of defectives is sufficient: two samples with the same count give identical likelihoods, whichever chairs failed. For normal data, the sample mean and variance together are sufficient. Other summaries can lose information. On the left, the sample mean and the sample median of twenty five normal seat heights, each over twenty thousand samples. Both centre on the true value, but the median is more spread out: its variance is about one and a half times the mean's, so it uses only about sixty five percent of the available information. It pays that price for resistance to outliers, a trade worth making when the normal model is doubtful. Sufficiency is always relative to a model, so keeping the full data matters when the model might be wrong. And some models break the usual regularity conditions: for a uniform distribution the maximum likelihood estimate is the sample maximum, which is biased and not normally distributed even in large samples. That completes the chapter. Next, a point estimate needs a calibrated statement of uncertainty and evidence.

This chapter builds intervals and tests, and keeps clear what each one claims, so that a threshold never substitutes for reasoning. Start with what confidence means. On the left, forty samples of thirty chairs each, from a population whose mean seat height is exactly four hundred and fifty millimetres. Each sample produces its own ninety five percent interval. The true mean never moves; the intervals do. Thirty five of these forty cover four hundred and fifty, and five, in pink, miss it. Over ten thousand such samples, ninety five point two percent cover it. That long run success rate is the interval's coverage, and it is what ninety five percent confidence means: a property of the procedure, under its assumptions. Intervals and tests are two views of the same procedure: a ninety five percent interval contains exactly the parameter values that a five percent test would not reject. A common misreading is to say there is a ninety five percent probability that the mean lies in a particular interval. Once computed, the interval either contains the fixed mean or it does not. A probability statement about the parameter itself needs a prior distribution, which is the Bayesian approach of chapter eleven. Next, intervals for a mean.

How should you put an interval around a sample mean? The standard tool is the t interval: the sample mean, plus or minus a t value times the standard error. The t value replaces the normal one point nine six because the standard deviation is estimated from the same data, and it comes from the t distribution with n minus one degrees of freedom. For the forty processing times, the mean is fourteen point oh seven minutes and the standard deviation ten point three eight. With thirty nine degrees of freedom the t value is two point oh two three, so the interval is fourteen point oh seven plus or minus three point three two: from about ten point eight to seventeen point four minutes. For normal data this procedure has exactly ninety five percent coverage at any sample size, the teal points on the left. For heavily skewed data it falls short: about eighty two percent at five observations, eighty nine percent at forty, still under ninety three at a hundred and sixty. The popular rule that thirty observations is enough is a rule of thumb. Processing times are skewed, with one extreme job, so this interval probably covers less than claimed. Next, the harder case of proportions.

Is the textbook interval for a proportion trustworthy? For proportions, coverage can be computed exactly: for each possible count, check whether its interval contains the true p, and add up the binomial probabilities of the counts that succeed. On the left, the exact coverage with forty inspected chairs, as the true defect rate varies. The textbook Wald interval, p hat plus or minus one point nine six standard errors, in pink, does badly for rare defects. At a one percent defect rate it covers the truth only a third of the time. The reasons show in the table. With no defectives among forty, Wald gives an interval of zero width, claiming certainty from nothing. With two defectives, its lower end is negative. The Wilson interval, in teal, inverts the score test and stays close to ninety five percent everywhere; its worst coverage here is ninety one. The Clopper Pearson interval, built directly from binomial tail probabilities, never covers less than ninety five percent, at the price of being wider. The jagged curves are real: counts are discrete, so no interval can be exactly ninety five percent for every p. For small counts, use Wilson or Clopper Pearson. Next, intervals for something other than a parameter.

Which interval answers the question you are actually asking? Three different targets get confused. A confidence interval targets a parameter, such as the mean seat height. A prediction interval targets a single future observation, such as the next chair off the line. A tolerance interval targets a stated share of the whole population, such as the range containing ninety five percent of chairs, with ninety five percent confidence. From the same twenty five seat heights, they are very different. The confidence interval for the mean is about plus or minus one and a half millimetres. The prediction interval for the next chair is about plus or minus seven. The tolerance interval is about plus or minus nine. As the sample grows, the confidence interval shrinks towards the true mean, because the mean is estimated ever more precisely. The other two do not shrink to nothing: they settle near the population's own spread, because individual chairs vary however much you sample. So if a customer asks whether their chair will fit within specification, the confidence interval is the wrong answer, by a factor of five. And the prediction and tolerance intervals lean directly on the normal shape of the tails. Next, testing.

Is the new timber supplier worse than the old one? A hypothesis test asks whether the data would be surprising if nothing had changed. That no change claim is the null hypothesis: the defect rate is still seven percent. The alternative, chosen before looking at the data, is that it has risen. A hundred and twenty chairs from the new supplier are inspected, and fourteen are defective. If the null hypothesis is true, the count follows a binomial distribution with mean eight point four, the reference distribution shown on the left. The p value is the probability, under that distribution, of a count at least as extreme as fourteen: the pink stems, adding up to about four percent. Fourteen is fairly far into the null distribution's tail, so this is moderate evidence that the rate has risen. Be precise about what a p value is. It is computed by assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and not the probability that the result is due to chance. And the direction of the alternative must be fixed in advance: choosing one sided after seeing which way the data lean halves the p value without justification. Next, what a p value cannot tell you.

Does a small p value mean an important effect? No. A p value blends the size of an effect with the amount of data, so it cannot by itself say whether anything matters. Here are three studies of a new glue that might shorten processing time, where a change of a minute or more would matter to the workshop. Study A ran two hundred thousand jobs per arm. It found a change of five hundredths of a minute, three seconds, with a p value of nought point oh three. Statistically significant, and practically trivial: the whole interval sits inside the shaded band of changes too small to matter. Study B ran only twenty jobs per arm. It estimated a minute and a half saving, but its interval runs from six minutes faster to three minutes slower, and the p value is about a half. Not significant, but not evidence of no effect either; it simply could not tell. Study C, with four hundred per arm, estimated the same minute and a half, with an interval from half a minute to two and a half. That one is clear and probably important. The lesson: report the estimate and its interval, and compare it with what matters. Next, planning a study to be informative.

How likely is a study to detect a change that really happened? Tests can err in two ways. A type one error rejects a null hypothesis that is true; the significance level alpha caps its rate. A type two error fails to reject a null that is false. Power is the probability of correctly detecting a given true effect. Return to the supplier test. With a hundred and twenty chairs, the exact test rejects when fourteen or more are defective, which keeps the false alarm rate at about four percent. But if the true rate has risen to ten percent, the test detects it only thirty one percent of the time, the pink curve on the left. The other sixty nine percent of the time, a real deterioration goes unnoticed. With four hundred and eighty chairs, the teal curve, power at ten percent rises to seventy five. Planning means fixing alpha, the change worth detecting, and the power wanted, then solving for the sample size: about five hundred and sixty chairs for eighty percent power against ten percent. Alternatively, plan for a target interval width. Either way, plan before collecting data. An underpowered study that finds nothing tells you very little. Next, ways the error rates are quietly broken.

When does a p value below five percent stop meaning what it says? The five percent error rate holds for one analysis, specified in advance. Break that and the rate climbs. Suppose the workshop tests twenty defect types for a change, when in truth none has changed. Each test has a five percent false alarm rate, but the chance that at least one of twenty raises an alarm is sixty four percent, the pink curve on the left. Reporting whichever came out significant is close to guaranteed to find something. A Bonferroni correction, testing each at a twentieth of five percent, restores an overall rate of about five percent. The second trap is optional stopping. Inspect chairs and run the test after every twenty, stopping as soon as it rejects. With no real change, the simulation shows a false alarm rate of sixteen and a half percent by four hundred chairs, against three percent for a single planned test. And when a test does not reject, say there is insufficient evidence, not that there is no effect. That completes the chapter. You can interpret coverage, choose an interval, and judge a test's evidence and error control. Next, specific data types and comparison units determine the right procedure.

This chapter matches common comparison procedures to what is being compared, to how the data depend on each other, and to the assumptions each method makes. The first question is always the design. Twelve boards were each glued twice, once with the old glue and once with the new, and the drying time recorded. On the left, each line is one board. The boards differ enormously, by up to eleven minutes, but within every board the new glue is faster. The two readings from the same board are strongly linked: their correlation is ninety six percent. These are paired data. A paired analysis works on the twelve within board differences. Their standard error is a quarter of a minute, and the evidence for a faster glue is overwhelming. Analyse the same twenty four numbers as if they came from twenty four separate boards, and the board to board variation swamps the comparison: the standard error grows fivefold and the p value is about one in five. Pairing removed the board variation from the comparison. The design determines the analysis. Choosing whichever analysis gives the smaller p value is not allowed, in either direction. Next, comparing two independent groups.

How do you compare two independent groups? Take processing times under two machine settings: fifteen jobs under A and twenty five under B. Setting B averages about three and a half minutes faster, but its times are far more variable: a standard deviation of four minutes against A's one and a half. The two sample t procedure divides the difference in means by its standard error. There are two versions. The pooled version assumes both groups share one variance and averages them. Welch's version estimates each group's variance separately and adjusts the degrees of freedom. Here they give different standard errors and intervals: Welch's interval runs from about one and a half to five and a quarter minutes. The bigger issue shows up in the table's last line. In a simulation where the true means are equal, with ten observations of high variance against forty of low variance, the pooled test raises a false alarm a quarter of the time instead of five percent. Welch's stays near five. Pooling fails badly when the smaller group is the more variable one. So use Welch by default; when variances really are equal, it loses almost nothing. Next, paired differences in detail.

Once data are paired, the analysis is simple: compute each unit's difference, and treat those differences as one sample. The twelve boards' differences, new glue minus old, are shown on the left. Their mean is minus one point six six minutes, with a standard deviation of under one minute. A t interval with eleven degrees of freedom, because there are twelve boards, runs from about minus two point two to minus one point one. The new glue saves between about one and two minutes a board. Now the trap. Suppose each board was read four times under each glue, giving forty eight reading differences. It is tempting to treat those as forty eight observations. That gives a standard error about thirty percent too small and a t statistic of eleven and a half instead of eight. The four readings of one board share that board's quirks, its wood, its joint, its position on the bench, so they are not independent replications of the comparison. They improve each board's measurement; they do not add boards. The experimental unit is whatever received the treatment, here the board. Average the readings within each board first, then analyse twelve differences. Next, comparing proportions.

Setting A produced thirty defective chairs out of four hundred, setting B eighteen. How should the difference be stated? There are three common measures. The absolute difference is three percentage points: one extra defective chair for every thirty three made. The relative risk is the ratio of the rates, one point six seven: A has sixty seven percent more defects. The odds ratio, one point seven two, compares odds rather than probabilities; it is close to the relative risk only when the rates are small, as here. Each needs its own interval. The difference's ninety five percent interval runs from slightly below zero to about six points, and the ratio intervals, computed on a log scale, run from just under one to about three. All three just include no difference, consistent with the chi square test's p value of seven percent. On the left, each rate with its own Wilson interval. A common mistake is to conclude from overlapping intervals that the rates are the same. Overlap of separate intervals is not the right test; use the interval for the difference. And report effects in more than one form: sixty seven percent more sounds much larger than three more per hundred. Next, larger tables.

Is defect status related to product type? The chi square test of independence answers that for a whole table. First compute the counts you would expect if product and defect status were independent: for each cell, the row total times the column total, divided by the grand total. Then add up, over all cells, the squared difference between observed and expected, divided by expected. For the thousand item table from chapter four, that sum is about seventeen and a half, with four degrees of freedom, giving a p value of about one and a half in a thousand. The variables are not independent. On the left, the Pearson residuals show which cells drive the result: tables have more minor and major defects than independence predicts, about one and a half times as many major ones. One caution concerns sparse cells. The chi square approximation needs expected counts of roughly five or more, and stools with a major defect are expected only about three times. A Monte Carlo version, shuffling defect labels while keeping the margins fixed, gives a p value of about two in a thousand, confirming the result. A significant test says the table departs from independence; the residuals say where, and the reason is a question of mechanism. Next, testing a model's fit.

Does the Poisson model of chapter three actually describe flaws on panels? A goodness of fit test compares the observed count in each category with the count the model predicts. Two hundred panels were inspected. They average one point four three flaws, but the variance is two point six two, much larger than the mean, which already warns against a Poisson, since a Poisson's variance equals its mean. Fit a Poisson with that mean anyway, and compare. On the left, the bars are observed panels and the dots are the Poisson's expected counts. There are too many flawless panels, too few with two flaws, and far too many with six or more. The chi square statistic is about fifty. The degrees of freedom need care. There are seven categories, so start from six, then subtract one more because the Poisson's mean was estimated from these same data, which pulls the fit closer than a model fixed in advance would be. Five degrees of freedom, and a p value of about one in a billion: the Poisson is clearly wrong. The likely reason is clustering, with some panels cut from bad sheets. And the six or more cell, expected under one, should be pooled or simulated. Next, comparing several groups at once.

With four machine settings, how do you compare their mean processing times without running six separate tests? Analysis of variance starts with one omnibus question: are all four means equal? It compares how far the group means spread around the overall mean with how much jobs vary within each group. If the group means differ by more than within group noise can explain, the ratio F is large. Here F is about eleven, with three and forty four degrees of freedom, and the p value is two in a hundred thousand. The means are not all equal. But the omnibus test does not say which differ, and it certainly does not say that every pair differs. On the left, settings one, two and four look alike, and setting three is slower. Making all six pairwise comparisons needs a multiplicity adjustment, as in chapter seven. With Bonferroni adjusted intervals, only the comparisons involving setting three exclude zero. Better still is a planned contrast, decided in advance: setting three against the average of the others, about two and three quarter minutes slower, with an interval from one point eight to three point seven. That completes the chapter. Next, credible treatment comparisons depend on experimental design and causal assumptions.

This chapter explains how an experiment's design supports claims about interventions, and why observational comparisons need extra assumptions. Start with what a causal effect is. Each batch has two potential outcomes: the defect rate it would have under setting A, and the rate it would have under setting B. The causal effect of B for that batch is the difference. The trouble is that a batch runs on one setting only, so one of the two outcomes is always unobserved, a counterfactual. Individual effects cannot be measured directly. On the left is a synthetic example where both outcomes are known, which never happens in practice. Every batch improves under B, by between one and two and a third points, and the average treatment effect is minus one point five seven five. Now run an experiment: randomly assign four batches to B. We see the bright points only, and the difference in observed means is minus one point three. Over all seventy possible random assignments, the difference averages exactly the true effect. That is what randomisation buys: an unbiased estimate of the average effect. But a single experiment can miss by more than a point, which is why replication matters. Next, the principles of good design.

What makes an experiment trustworthy? Four principles. Randomise: let chance, not an operator, decide which batches get which setting, so nothing systematic differs between the groups. Replicate: use enough units to estimate the noise as well as the effect. Block: group units that are alike, and randomise within each group, so known nuisance variation drops out of the comparison. And blind: keep whoever judges the outcome unaware of the treatment. Here is a setting experiment run over five days, four batches a day, with two batches each day drawn by lot for setting B. On the left, the days differ hugely, by about seven points in defect rate, as chapter one found. Because each day contains both settings, the comparison is made within days, and the day effects cancel. In a simulation with a true effect of minus point eight, a completely randomised design that ignores days gives estimates with a standard deviation of about point nine four; blocking by day cuts it to point four four, less than half. Blocking removes variation you can name in advance; randomisation protects against what you cannot. And blinding matters whenever a person makes a judgement call. Next, studying two factors at once.

How do you study two changes at once, a new glue and a new machine setting? Cross them. A factorial design runs every combination: setting A with old glue, A with new, B with old, B with new. Every run then informs both questions, which is more efficient than testing one factor at a time, and the design can reveal something one factor at a time cannot: an interaction. The main effect of the glue is its effect averaged over both settings. An interaction means the glue's effect depends on the setting. On the left are two scenarios. In the first, the lines are parallel: the new glue saves a minute and a half under either setting, so the effects simply add, and the interaction is zero. In the second, the lines cross: the glue saves a minute and a half under setting A but costs a third of a minute under B. The averaged main effect of the glue is then minus point six minutes, a number that describes neither setting. When factors interact, report the effect within each level. And this is exactly what changing one factor at a time can miss. Next, what goes wrong without randomisation.

What goes wrong when treatments are not randomised? Return to chapter one's observational month, where setting B looked worse overall. Operators chose the setting themselves, and they ran B mostly for tables. Tables are harder and fail more often whatever the setting. So product type affects both which setting a batch gets and whether it is defective. That makes it a confounder, and the diagram on the left shows the paths. The arrow from setting to defect is the effect we want. The path from setting back through product to defect is a back door, carrying association that is not causation. The crude comparison mixes both, and says B is worse by almost six points. Adjusting for product closes the back door. Within chairs, B is better by two points; within tables, by five. Standardised to an equal product mix, B is better by three and a half. But adjustment is only as good as the variables you measured. If operators also chose B for jobs that looked hard in some unrecorded way, the adjusted answer would still be confounded. Randomisation removes every arrow into the treatment, recorded or not, which is why it is the strongest design. Next, the assumptions observational analysis relies on.

What has to be true for a comparison to be read as cause and effect? Four assumptions. Consistency: setting B means one well defined intervention. If B is sometimes run fast and sometimes slow, its effect is not one thing. Overlap: every kind of unit could receive every treatment. Exchangeability: the groups receiving each treatment are comparable, with no unmeasured confounding; randomisation secures this by design. And no interference: one unit's treatment does not change another unit's outcome. On the left is overlap in the observational month. A quarter of chairs and three quarters of tables ran on setting B, so both products have data under both settings. Stools never ran on B at all. Nothing in the data can say how stools would fare under B; any estimate would be an extrapolation from a model, not evidence. Interference is easy to overlook. If batches share a kiln, running one batch hot could change the next batch's result, and then a batch's outcome depends on its neighbours' settings as well as its own. Randomisation helps with exchangeability, but the other three still need thought in every experiment. Next, what to do when units do not follow their assignment.

What happens when an experiment does not go to plan? Two hundred batches were randomised, a hundred to each setting. But operators, worried about jams, switched nine of the hardest batches assigned to B back to setting A. In this simulation the true effect of running B is a one point fall in defect rate. There are three ways to analyse it. Intention to treat compares the groups as randomised, keeping every batch where it was assigned. Per protocol drops the nine switched batches. As treated regroups batches by the setting they actually ran. On the left, the per protocol and as treated estimates are larger, about minus one and a half and minus one point seven, because both move hard batches out of the B group, leaving B with easier batches. That is confounding reintroduced after randomisation. Intention to treat keeps the randomised comparison intact.
