It answers a slightly different question, the effect of assigning B, which includes the reality that operators sometimes override it; its estimate, minus one point two five, is consistent with that. The effect of actually receiving B can be recovered by dividing by the compliance rate, under further assumptions. Next, planning an experiment properly.

How should the setting experiment be planned? Write the protocol before the first batch runs: the primary metric, the design, the analysis, the number of days, and the rule for stopping. Fixing these in advance means the results cannot steer the choices, which protects against the selective reporting and optional stopping of chapter seven. Sizing it uses the blocked design. Each day contributes one within day difference between B and A, with a variance of about one, so the standard error of the overall estimate is one over the square root of the number of days. To detect a fall of point eight points with eighty percent power, the experiment needs about fifteen days. The dots on the left are exact t test power; the curve is the normal approximation, which is optimistic for short experiments. Five days would give only about a twenty eight percent chance of detecting a real effect of that size. Finally, external validity. The experiment covers this product mix and this supplier. Its effect may differ for stools, or for new timber, and extending it needs an argument, not a p value. That completes the chapter. Next, regression extends comparisons to conditional relationships and adjustment.

This chapter interprets regression models and assesses their assumptions, uncertainty and scope. A regression is a model for a conditional mean: the average outcome among units with given predictor values. On the left, sixty jobs, with processing time against the number of parts. The fitted line is about three point three minutes, plus about one minute per part. It estimates the average time for jobs of each size; individual jobs scatter around it, with a typical residual of about two minutes, and some of those residuals are drawn in pink. Least squares chooses the intercept and slope that make the sum of squared residuals as small as possible, and the formulas come from the projection geometry in Linear Algebra. R squared, zero point eight four, is the share of the variation in time that the line accounts for. Note what least squares itself needs: nothing about distributions. It is a fitting rule. The standard errors and intervals that follow rest on further assumptions about the errors. And be careful with the intercept: three point three minutes for a job with no parts sits outside the data, which run from four to twenty parts. Next, more than one predictor.

What changes when a second predictor is added? Each coefficient now means the change in average time when that predictor moves by one, with the other predictors held fixed. Categories, like the type of wood, enter through an indicator: one for oak, zero for pine. With both in the model, the fitted equation is about two point nine, plus point nine nine per part, plus two point seven six for oak. On the left, that is two parallel lines: oak jobs take about two and three quarter minutes longer than pine jobs with the same number of parts. Adding the wood type also shrinks the residual scatter, from two point two to one point eight minutes. Could the per part time itself differ by wood? An interaction term, parts times oak, lets the slopes differ. Its estimate is minus point oh eight five with a standard error of point one one, so there is no evidence for different slopes, and the additive model is adequate. Two cautions. Holding the others fixed is a statement about the model; it is only informative where the data contain such comparisons. And coefficients change meaning with the company they keep. Next, predictors that carry the same information.

What happens when two predictors carry almost the same information? Each job's weight is roughly half its number of parts; on the left, the correlation is ninety nine percent. Fit either one alone and the answer is clear: about one minute per part, or about two minutes per kilogram, with small standard errors. Put both in the same model, and the coefficients become unstable. The parts coefficient's standard error jumps from point oh six to point four six, and the weight coefficient turns negative, minus point four six, with a standard error twice its size. The fitted values hardly change, because the model can trade one predictor against the other almost freely. The data simply cannot tell how the time divides between parts and weight. The variance inflation factor measures this: one over one minus the squared correlation, about sixty, so standard errors are inflated nearly eight times. A negative weight coefficient here does not mean heavier jobs are faster; it means the question of weight holding parts fixed has almost no information behind it, because weight barely varies once parts is known. Choose predictors for the question, or collect data where they vary separately. Next, the uncertainty in a fitted line.

How uncertain is a fitted line, and how uncertain is a prediction from it? These are different questions. A confidence interval for the mean response asks where the average time of all ten part jobs lies. A prediction interval asks where one new ten part job will fall, which adds that job's own scatter. On the left, the narrow orange band is the confidence band and the wide pink band the prediction band. At ten parts, the average time is between about thirteen and fourteen and a quarter minutes, but a single new job could take anywhere from about nine to eighteen. The confidence band is narrowest at the average number of parts and widens towards the edges, because the slope's uncertainty matters more far from the centre. The prediction band never shrinks below about two residual standard deviations, however much data you collect, because individual jobs vary. Beyond twenty parts, the shaded region, there are no data. At thirty parts the bands are only a little wider, but they assume the straight line continues, which the data cannot confirm. And these intervals rest on errors that are roughly normal, equal in variance and independent. Next, checking those assumptions.

How do you know whether a regression's assumptions hold? Look at the residuals. Three problems are common. Heteroscedasticity, spread that changes with the fitted value: in this second batch of jobs, residuals for small jobs have a standard deviation of about one and a half minutes, and for large jobs over four. The usual standard errors assume equal spread and are then wrong. Dependence: residuals that cluster by day, batch or time, as earlier chapters warned. And influence. On the left, one job with forty parts was logged at twenty minutes. It sits far beyond the other jobs in parts, so it has high leverage, eleven times the average, and it is far below the pattern. Together, that gives a Cook's distance of almost seven, when the next largest is under a third. It drags the slope from about one minute per part down to point seven two. Leverage alone is not a fault: an unusual job can be very informative. So investigate before deleting. Here the record shows a timer left running from another job. If a record cannot be checked, report the fit with and without it, and let readers see the difference. Next, getting the model's shape right.

What if the relationship is not a straight line? Look at batch assembly time against the number of chairs in a batch. The crew speeds up as a batch goes on, so each extra chair adds less time than the one before. A straight line, in pink on the left, misses that shape: it is too low for small batches and too high in the middle, and its residuals show a curved pattern. Using the logarithm of the number of chairs as the predictor straightens the relationship. The residual standard deviation drops from about two to one point six minutes, and the slope has a new meaning: about five and a half extra minutes for each doubling of the batch size. Now extrapolate to sixty chairs, twice the largest batch ever observed, in the shaded region. The straight line predicts fifty two minutes; the log model thirty five. In this synthetic example the truth is known, about thirty six, but in practice it is not. Both models fit the observed range reasonably well, and nothing in the data from two to thirty chairs can show which shape continues to sixty. Extrapolation rests on knowledge of the process or on new data. Next, outcomes that are counts or yes and no.

How should you model a yes or no outcome, like whether a chair is defective? A straight line can predict probabilities below zero or above one. Logistic regression instead models the log odds of a defect as a linear function of the predictors. On the left, four hundred chairs made at different machine speeds, with the observed defect rate in each speed band and the fitted logistic curve. The fitted coefficient for speed, point three three, means each extra chair per hour multiplies the odds of a defect by about one point three eight, with an interval from one point one four to one point six eight. On the probability scale the effect is not constant: the defect probability is about two percent at three chairs an hour and about ten percent at eight. Report results on the scale people use, with the caveat that the odds ratio is the constant part. Counts get the same treatment through Poisson regression, which models the log of a rate; it needs the exposure, such as panel area, so that bigger panels are not simply credited with more flaws. And it assumes the variance equals the mean, which chapter eight's clustered flaws violated. Next, the limits of what any regression shows.

What does a fitted regression actually establish? It describes conditional association in the data as collected. Two further steps need more. A causal claim, that changing a predictor would change the outcome, needs randomisation or a convincing argument that no unmeasured confounders remain, as chapter nine showed. A predictive claim, that the model will work on new jobs, needs validation on data not used to fit it, which the machine learning courses develop. A subtler problem is selection. Suppose ten candidate predictors are tried, none of them related to processing time, and the one with the largest t statistic is kept. On the left, its p value is below five percent about forty percent of the time, matching one minus point nine five to the tenth. With thirty candidates, nearly eighty percent. The p value of a selected variable ignores the search that found it. So report how the model was chosen, and treat discoveries from a search as leads for a confirmatory study. That completes the chapter. You can interpret coefficients and their uncertainty, diagnose failures, and separate association from causal and predictive claims. Next, Bayesian inference offers a different interpretation of parameter and predictive uncertainty.

This chapter explains posterior learning and distinguishes its interpretations from frequentist procedures. The idea is to describe uncertainty about a parameter itself with a probability distribution, and to update it with data using Bayes' rule, exactly as the screening test was updated in chapter two. Take the new chair supplier from chapter seven, with fourteen defective chairs in a sample of one hundred and twenty. Suppose, before inspecting, the workshop considered three possibilities: the new supplier is better, at four percent, the same, at seven percent, or worse, at ten percent, with prior probabilities one quarter, one half, and one quarter. The likelihood is the binomial probability of fourteen in one hundred and twenty under each rate: about two in ten thousand, two percent, and nine and a half percent. Multiply each prior by its likelihood and add; that total, point zero three four, is the marginal likelihood, the probability of the data averaged over the prior. Dividing by it gives the posterior: almost no belief left in better, thirty percent on same, and seventy percent on worse. The posterior is a statement about the rate, given a model and a prior.

Three hypotheses were a simplification: the defect rate could be any number between zero and one, so the prior should be a density. The beta family makes this easy. If the prior is a beta distribution with parameters a and b, and we observe x defectives in n chairs, the posterior is beta with parameters a plus x and b plus n minus x. In words, add the defectives to a and the good chairs to b. A useful reading follows: a beta prior behaves like a plus b chairs already inspected, a of them defective. On the left are two priors. The flat prior, beta one one, says every rate is equally plausible; after the data, its posterior is beta fifteen, one hundred and seven, with mean point one two three. The informed prior, beta two, twenty six, has mean point zero seven one, the old supplier's rate, and is worth about twenty eight chairs. Its posterior has mean point one zero eight, pulled a little towards seven percent. The data alone give point one one seven. With more inspections, the twenty eight prior chairs matter less and less, and the two posteriors converge.

A posterior is a whole distribution, so a report has to summarise it. Here is the informed posterior, beta sixteen, one hundred and thirty two. Its mean, median and mode are point one zero eight, point one zero six and point one zero three. They differ because the distribution is skewed to the right. The mode, also called the maximum a posteriori estimate, deserves a caveat. With zero defects in forty chairs and a flat prior, the mode is exactly zero, which suggests a perfect supplier, while the mean is point zero two four and the upper credible limit is seven percent. Reporting the mode alone hides the uncertainty. The shaded region is the ninety five percent credible interval, from point zero six four to point one six three. Its reading is direct: given the model and the prior, the rate lies in this range with probability point nine five. The Wilson confidence interval, from chapter seven, is similar in numbers but different in meaning: it describes how often the procedure covers the true rate across repeated samples. Neither reading transfers to the other. Finally, the posterior probability that the new supplier is worse than seven percent is point nine four seven, which is not a p value.

The workshop's real question is often about future chairs rather than the defect rate itself. How many of the next fifty chairs will be defective? A tempting shortcut is to plug in the estimate, point one zero eight, and use a binomial distribution. That treats the rate as known. The Bayesian answer averages the binomial forecast over the posterior: for each plausible rate, weight its forecast by how plausible the rate is. With a beta posterior, the result is a beta binomial distribution. On the left, pink shows the predictive and grey the plug in. Both have the same mean, five point four defectives in fifty. But the predictive is wider, with variance six point four against four point eight, because it includes the uncertainty about the rate as well as the chance variation of a batch. The difference shows in the tail. The probability of ten or more defectives is about four percent under the plug in, but six and a half percent under the predictive. If ten defectives in a batch triggers a costly recall, the plug in understates that risk by nearly half. Forecasts should carry parameter uncertainty forward.

A prior is an assumption, so treat it like one: state it, check it, and vary it. On the left, the same fourteen defectives in one hundred and twenty are combined with three priors. The flat prior and the light informed prior give posterior means of point one two three and point one zero eight. The third prior is sceptical: beta seventy, nine hundred and thirty, as if a thousand earlier chairs had shown exactly seven percent. That prior hardly moves. Its posterior mean is point zero seven five, and the probability that the supplier is worse falls from about point nine five to point seven three. Is such a prior reasonable? A prior predictive check asks what data the prior expected before seeing any. The sceptical prior expects eight point four defectives in one hundred and twenty, give or take three, and gives only about five percent probability to fourteen or more. The observed data sit in its tail, which suggests the old supplier's history may not describe the new one. A sensitivity analysis reports the conclusion under several priors. Here they all lean towards worse, but the strength of that conclusion depends on how much the old history is trusted.

Estimating the defect rate does not by itself say what to do. A decision needs the cost of each action under each possible rate. Next month the workshop will make two thousand chairs, and each defective chair costs eight pounds to repair. Keeping the new supplier therefore costs sixteen thousand times the defect rate. Switching back costs a three hundred pound fee plus the old supplier's seven percent, one thousand four hundred and twenty pounds in all. On the left, the amber line is the cost of keeping and the violet line the cost of switching. They cross at a break even rate of about point zero eight nine. Because the cost of keeping is linear in the rate, its expected cost under the posterior is sixteen thousand times the posterior mean. Under the flat and informed priors, that is one thousand nine hundred and sixty seven and one thousand seven hundred and thirty pounds, so switching back is cheaper. Under the sceptical prior it is one thousand two hundred pounds, and keeping wins. The loss function is a business judgement and the posterior is the evidence. Stating both separately shows which one drives the decision.

Conjugate priors are convenient, but most realistic priors and models are not conjugate. Suppose the quality engineer believes the new supplier is probably like the old one, but allows a twenty percent chance of a bad batch with a much higher rate. That prior is a mixture of two beta distributions, and no single update rule applies. The posterior is still prior times likelihood, divided by its total. With one parameter, we can evaluate that product at a grid of points and normalise, as the code does. The pink curve is the exact posterior, and the grey bars a grid of only twenty points. The coarse grid already gets the mean nearly right, point one one zero seven against point one one one zero. But the probability that the rate exceeds the break even value is point six five on twenty points, against point seven nine exactly. Tail probabilities converge much more slowly than means, so refine the grid until the answer stops changing. With many parameters, grids become impossible, and simulation methods take over. This completes the chapter. You can explain Bayesian updating and predictive uncertainty, compare prior sensitivity, and justify an elementary decision under a stated loss. Next, resampling and robust reasoning address limits of simple parametric analyses.

This chapter explains methods beyond simple parametric inference while keeping their assumptions and limits in view, and ends by evaluating a statistical argument as a whole. Every method so far began with a family of distributions: binomial, normal, Poisson. The empirical distribution begins with none. It places probability one over n on each observation, and lets the sample stand in for the population. Its cumulative distribution function, shown for the forty processing times from chapter one, is a staircase rising by one fortieth at each observed time. Any quantity defined on a distribution can be computed on this staircase. This is the plug-in principle. The mean is fourteen point one minutes, the median ten point seven five, the quartiles about nine and sixteen, and one job in ten took over twenty minutes. How close is the staircase to the truth? The grey band, from the Dvoretzky Kiefer Wolfowitz inequality, is plus or minus point two one five for forty observations, and covers the whole true curve at once with ninety five percent probability. Notice how wide that is. Nonparametric is not assumption free: the jobs must still be independent draws from one stable process.

The bootstrap applies the plug-in idea to uncertainty itself. To learn how a statistic would vary over repeated samples, draw new samples of the same size, with replacement, from the data, and recompute the statistic each time. The spread of those values estimates the standard error. The crucial choice is what to resample. The workshop's one hundred and twenty batch defect rates came from ten days, and batches made on the same day are alike. Resampling individual batches, in pink, treats them as one hundred and twenty independent units and gives a standard error of point two. Resampling whole days, in teal, matches how the data were gathered, and gives point six two, three times larger. Resample the unit that was sampled. From the bootstrap draws, several interval families are possible: the simple percentile interval, basic and studentised intervals, and the bias corrected and accelerated interval. They agree when the distribution is symmetric and differ when it is skewed. The bootstrap also fails in known places. For the maximum processing time, sixty four percent of resamples simply reproduce the observed maximum, because no resample can exceed the data. Extremes, very small samples and dependent data all need different methods.

A permutation test answers a testing question with almost no distributional assumptions. If the machine setting made no difference to processing times, the labels A and B would be arbitrary: any fifteen of the forty times could have carried the label A. So shuffle the labels, recompute the difference in means, and repeat. The grey histogram is five thousand such shuffles: the distribution of the difference when the null hypothesis is true. The observed difference, three point four one minutes, lies far in its tail; only about a third of one percent of shuffles were as extreme, so the p value is point zero zero three. The teal histogram is a bootstrap of the same difference, resampling within each group. It is centred at the estimate, not at zero, and gives a ninety five percent interval from one point seven to five point one. The permutation test asks whether there is any effect; the bootstrap asks how large it is. The shuffling is justified by exchangeability: under the null, the labels must be interchangeable. Here B is far more variable than A, so equal means alone do not make the labels exchangeable. When the settings were randomly assigned, the randomisation itself justifies the test.

Rank methods replace each value by its position in the combined sample. That makes them insensitive to outliers and to monotone changes of scale, such as taking logarithms. The Wilcoxon Mann Whitney test, applied to settings A and B, gives U of two hundred and eighty nine and a half, with a p value of about half a percent. But what does it estimate? Dividing U by fifteen times twenty five gives point seven seven: an estimate of the probability that a randomly chosen A job takes longer than a randomly chosen B job, with ties counted as half. It is often described as a test of medians, and that is wrong. On the left are two distributions with exactly the same median, twelve minutes, one skewed right and one skewed left. The probability that the first exceeds the second is point six, and with two hundred observations each the test rejects decisively. Only if the two distributions have the same shape, differing by a shift, does the test speak about a shift, and then the Hodges Lehmann estimate, three point three minutes here, summarises it. Rounded measurements produce ties, eight values here. They receive the average of their ranks, and the test variance is corrected.

Data contain mistakes. A timer left running over lunch, or a misplaced decimal point, produces one wild value, and a single wild value can move the mean anywhere. On the left, the longest of the forty processing times is moved from zero to three hundred minutes while the others stay fixed. The mean, in pink, follows it in a straight line without limit. The ten percent trimmed mean, which drops the four smallest and four largest values, stops moving once the value passes the others. So do the Huber estimate, which gives full weight to values near the centre and less weight to distant ones, and the median. The table pushes further, replacing the largest values by five hundred minutes. One bad value ruins the mean. The trimmed mean absorbs up to four, its ten percent, and the median nearly half. That fraction is the breakdown point. But robustness has a cost in meaning. For skewed processing times, the mean, the median and the trimmed mean are different quantities, not three estimates of one. If the question is the total time of the next forty jobs, only the mean answers it. Robust methods complement checking the data; they do not replace it.

Missing values are rarely missing at random in the everyday sense, and what they do to an analysis depends on why they are missing. Three mechanisms are distinguished. Missing completely at random means missingness is unrelated to anything. Missing at random means it is explained by variables that were recorded, here the job size, because large jobs more often lose their timing sheet. Missing not at random means it depends on the missing value itself, here the long jobs, perhaps because operators stop recording when a job overruns. The plot shows one simulated month, and the table a thousand. Under completely random missingness, simply analysing the complete cases is fine. Under missing at random, complete cases underestimate the mean, and their interval covers the truth in only thirteen percent of months. Filling the gaps with one regression prediction removes most of the bias but treats the guesses as real data, so its intervals are too narrow. Multiple imputation draws several plausible values, analyses each completed dataset, and adds the spread between them; it covers ninety six percent. Under missing not at random, no method using only the recorded data fixes the bias. Report how conclusions change across plausible departures.

Every analysis in this course involved choices: which test, which scale, whether to drop an unusual value, how to handle missing data. For settings A and B, six defensible analyses give p values between six in ten thousand and about half a percent. Here they agree, which is reassuring. But the danger lies in choosing among them after looking. In a simulation where the two settings are identical, a single planned Welch test rejects in five percent of datasets, as it should. Reporting whichever of the six gives the smallest p value rejects in nearly eleven percent. The p value of a chosen analysis ignores the choosing. The remedy is an analysis plan, written before the data are seen. It states the question and the quantity to be estimated, one primary analysis, the sensitivity analyses, the rules for exclusions, and how missing data will be handled. Departures from the plan are allowed, but labelled as exploratory. Reproducibility completes the plan: pin the code, the random seeds and the library versions, so another analyst gets the same numbers. And report every analysis that was run, with effects and intervals, not only the most striking result.

The course ends where any analysis should: with a report that says what the evidence supports. For settings A and B, the effect is that B processes jobs about three and a half minutes faster on average, with a bootstrap interval from one point seven to five point one minutes. Six different analyses agree, so the conclusion is not fragile to the choice of method. That is the strength of the evidence. Its limits must be stated just as plainly. The record does not show how jobs reached each setting, so a difference in job mix could explain part of the effect, as chapter nine warned. Setting B is also far more variable, which matters if deadlines are tight. And the population may have moved. The weekly defect rate stepped up from about seven to ten and a half percent when the timber supplier changed in week seven, so findings from before need checking after. This completes the course. You can match a resampling scheme to a design, identify robustness limits, reason about missing data, and communicate what a conclusion supports and what it leaves unresolved. Continue with unfamiliar examples and implementation practice, and use the companion courses for specialist depth.
